source: Clark & Brennan (1991) Grounding in communication
finding: Common ground is mutual knowledge that must be updated. The update process is called grounding. People stop when they reach the grounding criterion: the partners mutually believe the message was understood well enough for the current purpose.
numbers: No numbers. Core definition. The bar is 'sufficient for current purposes', not perfect understanding.
quote: The contributor and his or her partners mutually believe that the partners have understood what the contributor meant to a criterion sufficient for current purposes.
limits: Theory chapter. The criterion is not directly measured in this chapter.
agent_relevance: Our agent has no grounding criterion. It could set a task-sized bar for 'understood well enough' before acting, and raise it for high-stakes steps.

source: Clark & Brennan (1991) Grounding in communication
finding: Principle of least collaborative effort: both partners try to minimise the total work from starting a contribution to its mutual acceptance. It replaces the older 'least effort for the speaker' idea. Three problems with the old idea: time pressure, errors, and ignorance of the partner. Speakers therefore issue rough utterances and let the partner help (try markers, installments, invited completions).
numbers: No numbers. Example from Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs 1986: 'the person ice skating that has two arms?' said with rising intonation.
quote: In conversation, the participants try to minimize their collaborative effort--the work that both do from the initiation of each contribution to its mutual acceptance.
limits: Principle derived from observation, not a new experiment.
agent_relevance: A single agent talking to a user should not polish one long answer. A cheap provisional answer with a check-in can cost less in total than a perfect answer to a misread request.

source: Clark & Brennan (1991) Grounding in communication
finding: Grounding has levels. Evidence that a message got through comes in kinds (continued attention, relevant next turn, acknowledgement, demonstration, display of the words). Different purposes need different strength of evidence. Verbatim registration is used for phone numbers, in installments.
numbers: Geluykens (1988) cited: 29% of left-dislocated noun phrases in the London-Lund corpus are followed by an intervening move by the partner; another 52% by a pause where the partner could nod. Directory-enquiry installments of 3-4 digits.
limits: Numbers are secondary citations inside the chapter, not new data.
agent_relevance: A schema could tag each handoff with the evidence it needs: none, restate, or run-and-show-result.

source: Clark & Brennan (1991) Grounding in communication
finding: Grounding costs depend on the medium. Eight medium constraints: copresence, visibility, audibility, cotemporality, simultaneity, sequentiality, reviewability, revisability. Eleven costs: formulation, production, reception, understanding, start-up, delay, asynchrony, speaker change, display, fault, repair.
numbers: Eight constraints and eleven costs, listed in the chapter. Table 1 rates seven personal media.
limits: Qualitative table. Chapter predates chat with LLMs. The cost list is not an empirical scale.
agent_relevance: A text-only LLM chat has no copresence, visibility or audibility. Extra grounding techniques must be explicit in text.

source: Cohen (1984), as reported in Clark & Brennan (1991)
finding: Tutors guiding students to assemble a pump did more separate identify-then-instruct turns by telephone than by keyboard. On keyboard they identified the object and gave the instruction in one turn. Clark and Brennan explain this by the cost profile of each medium.
numbers: Counts not given in the chapter. Direction only: many more separate identification requests by phone.
limits: Read secondhand. Small 1984 lab study. Explanation is post hoc.
agent_relevance: When each turn is costly (slow, batch, tool call), people pack more into one turn and risk more misunderstanding. Our scaffold calls are costly turns, so check-ins must be planned.

source: Klein, Feltovich, Bradshaw, Woods (2005) Common ground and coordination in joint activity
finding: Joint activity needs a Basic Compact: a usually tacit agreement to coordinate, align goals, stay predictable, repair faulty beliefs when detected, and signal if one drops out. The compact varies in strength and is renewed, not given once.
numbers: Three requirements: interpredictability, common ground, directability. Common ground has three parts: initial common ground, public events so far, current state of the activity.
quote: Joint activity assumes a basic compact, which is an agreement (often tacit) to facilitate coordination and prevent its breakdown.
limits: Conceptual paper built from incidents, not an experiment. Clancey (2004) is cited as arguing agent teamwork is too shallow to call collaboration.
agent_relevance: If the LLM is a team member it must honour the compact: tell the user when it cannot continue, and say what it assumed.

source: Klein, Feltovich, Bradshaw, Woods (2005) Common ground and coordination in joint activity
finding: Common ground is a process of communicating, testing, updating, tailoring and repairing mutual understanding, not a stored state of having the same knowledge. Quality varies with purpose (chit-chat vs a contract). Six support activities: structure preparation, sustain, update, monitor, detect anomalies, repair.
numbers: Six activities listed. Five kinds of mutual knowledge named: roles, routines, skills, goals and commitment, stance (time pressure, fatigue, competing priorities).
limits: Taxonomy from reviewing team coordination. Not tested against data in the paper.
agent_relevance: Maps to a shared-state checklist for a user-agent pair: who owns what, what the agent can do, what the goal is, what the agent assumes.

source: Klein, Feltovich, Bradshaw, Woods (2005) Common ground and coordination in joint activity
finding: The Fundamental Common Ground Breakdown: A believes B has some knowledge. B lacks it and does not know he should have it, so he does not ask. His silence looks to A like confirmation. Later statements are then read under the wrong assumption and errors cascade.
numbers: Worked incidents: Viennese Waltz (the word 'presentation' meant the whole talk to the speaker and only a slide file to the assistant; handouts almost not sent), Fuel Leak (pilot asked 'Are you having any trouble?', answer 'No', leak diagnosis took another ten minutes), Handing off an Airplane (reroute lost at an air traffic hand-off).
quote: Party B doesn't have this knowledge, and doesn't know he is supposed to have it. Therefore, he or she doesn't request it.
limits: Anecdotes collected by the authors, not a sample with a rate. No base rate given.
agent_relevance: The best-fit human failure for an LLM that does not ask. An agent that never queries a vague term produces exactly the silence that looks like agreement.

source: Klein, Feltovich, Bradshaw, Woods (2005) Common ground and coordination in joint activity
finding: The joint action ladder (after Clark 1996): attend, perceive, understand, act. A message can fail at any rung. Higher rungs give 'downward evidence' for lower ones, so a relevant reply shows the earlier rungs worked. A bare acknowledgement does not prove understanding.
numbers: Four rungs. Examples: a virus disabling a colleague's email; a hurried reader never reading the detail.
limits: Descriptive. Rungs are not operationalised for measurement in this paper.
agent_relevance: A check could ask the agent to restate the request and act on one concrete step, not just say 'got it'.

source: Klein, Feltovich, Bradshaw, Woods (2005) Common ground and coordination in joint activity
finding: Coordination has costs, and the effort to choreograph joint activity is itself a cost. Shared scripts and signalling cut that cost: for example one word 'stick' in a relay hand-off. Diversity of perspective can improve performance but needs more repair.
numbers: No numbers. Relay-race hand-off is the running example.
limits: Argument by example. The diversity claim cites other work (Feltovich 1996; Spiro 1989).
agent_relevance: Terse protocols between our modules are good only if prior common ground exists. Where it does not, expand.

source: Klein, Feltovich, Bradshaw, Woods (2005) Common ground and coordination in joint activity
finding: For software as team member: automation should be designed to the requirements of the Basic Compact, to be predictable, directable, and to show status and intent. Earlier agent research focused on autonomy; newer research turns to joint activity.
numbers: Section 6 of the paper. The ten-challenges list is developed in the companion 2004 IEEE Intelligent Systems piece.
limits: Position paper. Clancey (2004) argues machines lack the commitment that makes human teamwork.
agent_relevance: Direct design guidance for agent-user and agent-agent handoffs. Background only for our single agent.

source: Klein, Woods, Bradshaw, Hoffman, Feltovich (2004) Ten challenges for making automation a team player in joint human-agent activity
finding: Ten challenges for automation as a teammate: enter a basic compact, model others, be predictable, be directable, reveal status and intentions, interpret signals, negotiate goals, support collaborative planning, manage attention, control coordination costs.
numbers: Ten items. Titles read; full wording not read (page truncated). IEEE Intelligent Systems 19, 91-95; DOI 10.1109/MIS.2004.74.
limits: Only the item titles were read from a reader page. No empirical test in the article.
agent_relevance: Use as a checklist. Items 5 (reveal status) and 7 (goal negotiation) are the ones most missing in today's LLM agents.

source: Keysar, Barr, Balin, Brauner (2000) Taking perspective in conversation: the role of mutual knowledge in comprehension
finding: Eye tracking shows addressees do not restrict reference resolution to what both people can see. They look at, and sometimes reach for, an object the director cannot see. Mutual knowledge is used as a late correction, not as an early filter.
numbers: Exp 1: 20 addressees, 4x4 shelf with occluded slots. Fixations on occluded object: 1.01 test vs 0.65 control; total time 420 ms vs 178 ms. Addressees reached or grabbed the hidden object in 23% of test trials (none in control). Exp 2: 40 addressees; fixations 0.90 vs 0.33; time 452 vs 106 ms; hidden object reached for or grabbed in 20% of test trials vs once in control. Decision lag 2,092 vs 1,146 ms (Exp 1).
quote: addressees can be lax in their use of common ground
limits: Scripted confederate director, simple array, one task. Does not show people never use common ground, only that it is applied late and with errors.
agent_relevance: People and models alike start from their own view, then adjust. For an LLM, the hidden-information trap is real: it answers from its own context unless forced to model the partner's view.

source: Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs (1986) Referring as a collaborative process
finding: Tangram matching: a director describes abstract figures, a matcher picks them. Referring is a joint act: present a description, the partner accepts or refashions it (replace, expand, repair), and the agreed description joins the common ground. Descriptions get shorter across repeated trials.
numbers: Not opened (the PDF host failed a certificate check). Exact words-per-trial and turn counts not verified and not recorded here.
limits: Source unread by me. Only the model as described in Heeman & Hirst 1995 and Clark & Brennan 1991 is used.
agent_relevance: Repeated tasks with the same partner should converge to short agreed labels. Our agent could keep an agreed-terms list per user.

source: Heeman & Hirst (1995) Collaborating on referring expressions
finding: First computational model of Clark and Wilkes-Gibbs. Conversation moves are plan operators: initial presentation, judgment (accept, reject, postpone), and refashioning by replace-plan or expand-plan. Plans are parsed by a chart parser over actions, not words, so a collaborative reference ends only when both sides accept.
numbers: Algorithm with discourse plans and worked examples. No human-subject numbers.
limits: Toy domain, hand-built plans. No test on spontaneous dialogue at scale.
agent_relevance: A small state machine for referent negotiation (present, judge, refashion) is cheap to run in code. It matches our rule that the program decides transitions.

source: Brennan & Clark (1996) Conceptual pacts and lexical choice in conversation
finding: Speakers who repeatedly refer to an object settle on a term with a specific partner. Changing the term for the same object costs the listener, and the pact is partner-specific. Later work found pacts are fluid when goals change.
numbers: Not opened (PDF fetch blocked). No numbers recorded.
limits: Unverified recollection only. Do not quote numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Keep a per-conversation glossary of agreed terms and do not silently rename things in later turns.

source: Shaikh, Gligoric, Khetan, Gerstgrasser, Yang, Jurafsky (2024) Grounding gaps in language model generations (NAACL)
finding: LLMs presume common ground instead of building it. Against human replies in the same dialogue context, LLM generations are on average 77.5% less likely to contain a grounding act (clarification, follow-up, acknowledgement).
numbers: Datasets: ESConv, TSCC, P4G. Few-shot GPT-4 classifier macro-F1 0.89 across datasets. Average decreases: follow-ups 64.3%, acknowledgements 83.4%, clarifications down 84.8% on TSCC. ChatGPT-3.5 on ESConv: follow-up base rate 10.76, acknowledgement 1.05, clarification 0.
quote: off-the-shelf LLM generations are, on average, 77.5% less likely to contain grounding acts than humans
limits: Simulated next-turn only, one turn at a time, 2023-era models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Mistral, Llama). Agreement with humans poor to fair (Cohen kappa below 0.2 for most).
agent_relevance: Strong support: base LLMs skip the grounding act. Our agent needs an explicit clarify state with a code-checked trigger.

source: Shaikh, Gligoric, Khetan, Gerstgrasser, Yang, Jurafsky (2024) Grounding gaps in language model generations (NAACL)
finding: Cause test: supervised instruction tuning does not raise grounding, and preference optimisation lowers it. In the preference data, assistant replies with questions are less preferred.
numbers: Mistral 7B SFT on UltraChat, 3 epochs, 10 checkpoints: no correlation of kappa with steps (p>0.1). DPO on UltraFeedback: kappa falls with steps, Pearson R about -0.79 (p<0.05 for all acts). Archangel PPO: base rate -7.0%, kappa -39.0%; DPO: -12.1%, -42.5%. Questions occur in 13.77% of preferred vs 18.35% of dispreferred UltraFeedback examples (chi2=484.08).
limits: Correlational across checkpoints; one small base model for the ablation; synthetic preference data.
agent_relevance: Reward-model style training pushes agents to answer, not ask. Our scaffold should not rely on the model's own taste to ask.

source: Shaikh, Gligoric, Khetan, Gerstgrasser, Yang, Jurafsky (2024) Grounding gaps in language model generations (NAACL)
finding: Prompting the model to ground fixes the rate but not the quality: over-grounding. A mitigation prompt on ChatGPT-3.5 raised ESConv follow-ups from 10.76 to 42.32 and acknowledgements from 1.05 to 2.54, yet agreement with humans stayed poor.
numbers: Clarification kappa went from 0 to -1.65 (worse than chance). Follow-ups ran about 50% above the human supporter rate.
limits: One prompt, one model, one dataset family. Asking more is not asking at the right time.
agent_relevance: An 'ask more questions' instruction is not enough. The trigger for asking must come from a check (missing slot, conflicting reading), not from volume.

source: Li, Chong, Stepputtis, Campbell, Hughes, Lewis, Sycara (2023) Theory of mind for multi-agent collaboration via large language models (EMNLP)
finding: In a text team game (find and defuse bombs), LLM agents show emergent teamwork but fail from long-context loss and hallucinated task state. An explicit written belief state raises both task efficiency and ToM accuracy.
numbers: Team score (max 90): ChatGPT 43, GPT-4 90. Rounds to finish: ChatGPT 30.0, GPT-4 12.3, GPT-4 + belief 11.0 (MAPPO 30.0). ToM probes introspection / first-order / second-order: ChatGPT 79.0 / 41.9 / 11.6; GPT-4 80.0 / 60.0 / 64.3; GPT-4+Belief 97.2 / 80.1 / 69.4 (%). Valid actions: ChatGPT 62.5%, GPT-4 86.1%. Belief state cut invalid actions 50.7% and raised team efficiency 130% (as reported).
limits: Small game, few trials (std 0.0 on scores), GPT-3.5/4 era, belief probes annotated by the experimenters.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a written shared-belief record: it helped agents track what others know. Fits our counted-state idea.

source: Cemri, Pan, Yang et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: A taxonomy of 14 failure modes in three groups from 1,642 annotated traces of 7 multi-agent frameworks. Several are coordination and common-ground failures: failing to ask for clarification, information withholding, ignoring another agent's input, reasoning-action mismatch.
numbers: 1,642 traces, 7 frameworks (ChatDev, MetaGPT, AppWorld and others). Group shares: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%. Per mode in main text: fail to ask for clarification 6.80%; information withholding 0.85%; ignored other agent's input 1.90%; reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%. System failure rates 41% to 86.7%. Annotator kappa 0.88; LLM judge kappa 0.77, accuracy 94%.
limits: Mostly GPT-4-family traces. Per-mode percentages differ between figure and text in different versions. Modes overlap.
agent_relevance: Our agent still has internal handoffs between roles. Use these modes as test cases for the scaffold: clarify, withhold, ignore, mismatch.

source: Cemri, Pan, Yang et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Prompt-level fixes help only a little. A change to the workflow (making the CEO agent the final say) raised ChatDev task success by 9.4% with the same model. A verification step raised ProgramDev success by 15.6% for ChatDev.
numbers: +9.4% task success (ChatDev, GPT-4o, same user prompt); +15.6% on ProgramDev with verification (appendix H).
limits: Gains are against a weak baseline. The authors say such fixes are not enough for reliability.
agent_relevance: Structure and checks beat prompt reminders for coordination failures. Matches our rule that code, not the model, moves the state.

source: Shao et al. (2026) Collaborative Gym: a framework for enabling and evaluating human-agent collaboration (ICLR)
finding: Human-agent collaboration beats fully autonomous agents on three tasks, and the main failures are communication and situational awareness, i.e. common-ground failures.
numbers: Win rates vs autonomous agent with real users: Travel Planning 86%, Tabular Analysis 74%, Related Work 66%. Failure rates in real condition: communication 65%, situational awareness 40% (simulated: 80% and 47%). Sub-failures: agent works without telling the user (C.1, 23%), no progress or completion updates (C.3, 29%), ignores session context (SA.1, 11%), fails to merge several user messages (SA.3, 13%).
limits: Three tasks, mostly GPT-4o-class backbones, small human samples (20 users per ablation).
agent_relevance: The user-facing failures concern status and shared state, not task skill. Our output should always state what it assumed and what it did not do.

source: Shao et al. (2026) Collaborative Gym: a framework for enabling and evaluating human-agent collaboration (ICLR)
finding: Non-turn-taking interaction, where either side can act and a notification tells the other, was preferred to strict turn-taking with the same agent.
numbers: 20 professional users per task. Travel Planning: task performance 0.84 vs 0.81, satisfaction 3.95 vs 3.55 (p=0.012), win rate 70%. Tabular Analysis: performance 0.81 vs 0.79, satisfaction 4.25 vs 3.55, win rate 70%.
limits: n=20 per task. Same agent (gpt-4o) in both versions; only the interaction paradigm differed.
agent_relevance: A visible shared workspace can reduce grounding cost. Our single-agent loop is turn-based, so a visible state log is the nearest equivalent.

source: Khebour, Lai, Bradford, Zhu, Brutti, Tam, Tu, Ibarra, Krishnaswamy, Pustejovsky (2024) Common ground tracking in multimodal dialogue (LREC-COLING)
finding: A formal common ground structure tracks what a group jointly accepts. It has FBank (facts), EBank (evidence for and against), and QBank (questions under discussion). A neural move classifier feeds closure rules that update the banks.
numbers: Move classification weighted F1 0.61 averaged across groups; main errors confuse STATEMENT and ACCEPT. Annotation agreement: action F1 0.67; common-ground annotation F1 0.54. Weight-estimation task, 10 groups.
limits: Small dataset (10 groups), one task (guess block weights), pre-LLM-agent design. Misclassifying acceptance changes the evidence level, not the content.
agent_relevance: A direct template for a shared-belief store: facts, evidence, open questions. Our agent could keep those three lists per task.

source: Zhu, Bradford, Lai, Obiso, Venkatesha, Pustejovsky, Krishnaswamy (2026) Distributed Partial Information Puzzles: examining common ground construction under epistemic asymmetry
finding: Prompted LLMs struggle to infer the group's shared beliefs from multimodal updates in a task where three directors each hold partial information. Their output often differs from a formal Dynamic Epistemic Logic pipeline.
numbers: Dice similarity to the axiomatic common ground, Actions-to-Structure setting: Llama-3.2-3B average 0.219, Qwen3-4B 0.276, GPT-5-mini/GPT-5 0.382. Global scores 0.049, 0.107, 0.363. In the failed Group 7, Qwen and GPT matched the axiomatic common ground at 1.000 because little was shared.
limits: Small models plus GPT-5-mini; one construction task; few groups. The perfect Group 7 score reflects emptiness, not skill.
agent_relevance: Rule-based tracking of what has been jointly confirmed beats LLM guesses. Use code to hold the common-ground record.

source: Li, Gatt, Poesio (2026) Seeing is not sharing: some vision-language models overestimate common ground in asymmetric dialogue
finding: Giving a model both maps raises accuracy but makes it over-predict that understanding is shared. Seeing what could be shared is taken as proof that it was shared.
numbers: 13,077 annotated reference expressions from HCRC MapTask. Gold: 72.1% aligned. Qwen3-VL-8B, both maps: macro-F1 .591 to .671, but recall on aligned .590 to .822 and recall on not-aligned .677 to .518; yes-rate .515 to .727. Blank or shuffled maps give yes-rate about .18 to .19.
limits: One main model; five models in total. Task is an overhearer-style judgment, not live dialogue.
agent_relevance: Having the same context in the prompt does not equal common ground. A check must require evidence from the exchange.

source: Sarkar, Srikanth, Gupta, Bonial, Resnik, Rudinger (2026) Sycophancy undermines epistemic vigilance in cooperative vision-language tasks
finding: In an information-asymmetric spot-the-difference game, vision-language models agree with their partner against their own private image. Common ground is wrongly updated by deferral.
numbers: Qwen3-VL-32B as Player 2 made at least one epistemic vigilance violation in more than 40% of conversations (45.3% ANALYSIS, 47.1% TEST). Anti-sycophancy activation steering cut this to 31.3% (p=0.001) and 39.1% (p=0.003); a guardrail prompt only to 44.0% and 44.1%. TEST balanced accuracy rose from 65.2 to 72.0 with steering.
limits: One main open model; steering vector from other work; ANALYSIS set small, TEST n=399.
agent_relevance: Agreement bias corrupts the shared record. Agent-to-agent checks should test each claim against private evidence before accepting.

source: Ahuja, Li, Lampinen (2026) Beneath the surface: investigating LLMs' capabilities for communicating with subtext
finding: Frontier models communicate too literally. They can use stated common ground to hint, but fail to infer whether common ground exists when it is not stated.
numbers: Best models gave literal clues 60% of the time in Visual Allusions. With explicit common ground, some models cut overly literal clues by 30%-50%. Scores when they had to infer common ground were roughly 2x lower than the best.
limits: Dixit-like games and allegories; early-2026 frontier models. Creativity measures are subjective.
agent_relevance: Models do not build a model of what the partner knows by themselves. State it for them.

source: Chen, Sun, Lu, Wang, Wang, Yao (2026) CollabSim: a CSCW-grounded methodology for investigating collaborative competence of LLM agents
finding: A simulation framework takes classic human-team tasks (Shape Factory, DayTrader, Hidden Profile, Map Task) and varies communication bandwidth, visibility, and group size, with probes of agent internal states. It argues agents fail through weak collaboration, not weak task skill.
numbers: Four tasks, four LLMs (Qwen3.6-35B, Llama-4-Maverick, GPT-5.5, Claude 4.6). In one Map Task cell, Claude 4.6 route accuracy was 0.45 (persona prompt) vs 0.72 (theory-informed prompt). DayTrader cooperation rate ranged from 0% to 83% across models and prompts.
limits: Few runs per cell; numbers vary widely. Read the tables cautiously.
agent_relevance: The useful part is the measurement idea: probe belief about the partner at each step, not only final outcome.

source: Mishra, Arvan, Zalake (2026) TeamMedAgents: Pareto-efficient multi-agent medical reasoning through teamwork theory
finding: A multi-agent scaffold built from Salas's teamwork theory (shared mental models, leadership, orientation, trust, mutual monitoring) reaches competitive accuracy for small models at lower token cost than other multi-agent systems.
numbers: Eight medical benchmarks. Average accuracy 49.4% for the full-component version vs 48.4-51.6% for MedAgents, DyLAN, ReConcile, MDAgents. The shared mental model is updated at the end of each turn.
limits: Small models (about 4B); competitive, not clearly better; ablations on 50-question samples.
agent_relevance: Weak support. A shared mental model record is cheap, but the accuracy gain is not clear in this paper.

source: Krauss & Weinheimer (1964) Changes in reference phrases as a function of frequency of usage in social interaction
finding: Early referential-communication result: as pairs repeat references to the same abstract figures, their phrases get shorter and settle. A precursor to the tangram work.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Unverified recollection. Cited only as the origin of the repeated-reference paradigm.
agent_relevance: Repeated work with one user should converge. If it does not, that is a signal of lost common ground.

source: Horton & Keysar (1996) When do speakers take into account common ground?
finding: Speakers also start from what is easy for themselves. Under time pressure they design messages less for the partner. This is the production-side match to Keysar et al. 2000.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Unverified recollection. A competing account to full audience design.
agent_relevance: Time pressure or short budgets will push our agent to skip partner modelling. Protect that step in the budget.
